description: Defines how A.R.I.A. selects, scores, executes, evaluates, and reroutes diagnostic next hops through a dynamic microwave backhaul reasoning graph.

core_principle.statement: ARIA shall select the diagnostic next hop expected to produce the greatest useful reduction in uncertainty or advancement toward resolution for the lowest justified operational cost, risk, and disruption.
rules: The most probable hypothesis does not automatically determine the next action.
The cheapest action does not automatically determine the next action.
The highest-information action does not automatically determine the next action.
Routing shall balance diagnostic value against operational cost and constraints.
Every completed action changes the current routing state.
ARIA reroutes from the resulting state rather than restarting a predetermined troubleshooting tree.
Graph topology may change as evidence is received.
Edge weights are dynamic rather than permanent universal values.
The same diagnostic action may have different route value in different cases.
A previously poor route may become valuable when context changes.
Candidate actions shall have a defined diagnostic purpose.
ARIA shall not generate actions merely because they appear in a generic troubleshooting procedure.
Actions incompatible with the current technical context shall be excluded.
Actions prohibited by safety or authorization constraints shall not be executable candidates.
Questions are valid diagnostic actions when the answer has meaningful expected information value.

routing_dimensions.name: EXPECTED_INFORMATION_GAIN
routing_dimensions.description: Expected reduction in meaningful diagnostic uncertainty.

routing_dimensions.name: DIAGNOSTIC_DISCRIMINATION
routing_dimensions.description: Ability of the action's possible outcomes to distinguish between competing hypotheses.

routing_dimensions.name: HYPOTHESIS_COVERAGE
routing_dimensions.description: Amount of relevant active hypothesis space affected by the action.

routing_dimensions.name: TIME_COST
routing_dimensions.description: Expected time required to perform the action and obtain usable evidence.

routing_dimensions.name: EXECUTION_COST
routing_dimensions.description: Financial or resource cost of executing the action.

routing_dimensions.name: PHYSICAL_EFFORT
routing_dimensions.description: Human effort required to perform the action.

routing_dimensions.name: SERVICE_IMPACT
routing_dimensions.description: Potential disruption to live network service.

routing_dimensions.name: SAFETY_RISK
routing_dimensions.description: Potential safety consequence associated with the action.

routing_dimensions.name: INVASIVENESS
routing_dimensions.description: Degree to which the action modifies the current technical state merely to obtain information.

routing_dimensions.name: REVERSIBILITY
routing_dimensions.description: Ease with which the technical state can be restored after the action.

routing_dimensions.name: HISTORICAL_EFFECTIVENESS
routing_dimensions.description: Validated historical ability of the action to advance similar cases.

routing_dimensions.name: USER_CAPABILITY
routing_dimensions.description: Likelihood that the current user can correctly perform the action and return reliable evidence.

routing_dimensions.name: CONTEXT_APPLICABILITY
routing_dimensions.description: Technical applicability of the action to the current equipment, configuration, scope, and case state.

routing_dimensions.name: RESULT_AVAILABILITY
routing_dimensions.description: Likelihood that the requested action can actually produce usable evidence under current conditions.

rules: Weight values shall remain configurable.
Weights may vary by operational context.
Safety constraints may act as hard gates rather than ordinary weighted penalties.
Service-impact constraints may act as hard gates where applicable.
ARIA shall preserve the component scores used to calculate route utility.

information_gain.description: ARIA shall prefer actions whose possible outcomes are expected to meaningfully reduce uncertainty among important hypotheses.
rules: Information gain shall consider all materially likely action outcomes.
A test that returns the same expected result under every major hypothesis has low discriminatory value.
A test capable of sharply separating competing hypotheses may have high information value even when it does not directly fix the problem.
Information gain estimates may initially be qualitative when empirical outcome probabilities are unavailable.
ARIA should predict diagnostically meaningful possible outcomes before requesting an action when practical.
Actual outcomes shall be compared against expected outcomes.
Unexpected results shall trigger rerouting rather than being discarded.

action_cost_classes.name: MODERATE
examples: Access equipment requiring additional field effort

cheap_test_preference.rule: When multiple actions provide comparable diagnostic value, ARIA should prefer the action requiring less time, effort, risk, cost, and service disruption.

example.interpretation: This action may outrank testing a 55 percent physical RF hypothesis when physical verification requires a tower climb.

high_consequence_policy.description: Low-probability hypotheses may justify early investigation when failure consequences are severe and the available test is proportionate.
rules: Probability alone shall not determine diagnostic priority.
Expected consequence may modify route priority.
Safety-critical conditions may require immediate evaluation regardless of ordinary route score.
Low-probability high-consequence hypotheses should not trigger disproportionate invasive action without justification.

user_adaptive_routing.description: ARIA may adapt diagnostic route selection according to validated history of how individual users perform diagnostic actions and provide evidence.
rules: User adaptation shall improve route efficiency rather than punish or stereotype users.
User-specific route effects shall be based on validated experience.
User capability shall be contextual to the action.
ARIA may provide more explicit instructions when historical evidence indicates that doing so improves result quality.
User-specific routing shall not override safety or technical truth.
ARIA may request multiple actions in parallel when they are independent, low-cost, and operationally efficient.
Parallel actions should not create unnecessary workload.
Actions whose interpretation depends on earlier results should remain sequential.
ARIA shall preserve which evidence resulted from which parallel branch.
An action requiring unavailable prerequisite information shall be deferred.
Prerequisite actions may receive increased route value when they unlock multiple downstream diagnostic routes.
ARIA shall avoid requesting information that can already be derived reliably from existing evidence.
Dependencies shall be represented explicitly rather than hidden in conversational instructions.
A completed valid diagnostic action shall normally receive a substantial repeat penalty.
Repeating an action requires an explicit reason.
A repeated action after a meaningful technical change is not considered redundant.
ARIA shall recognize semantically equivalent actions to prevent disguised loops.

route_failure_learning.description: Diagnostic routes that fail to produce useful information shall influence future route selection without becoming permanently prohibited.
rules: Low-yield actions may receive reduced future route value in similar contexts.
An action may remain valuable in other contexts.
Failure to confirm the tested hypothesis does not mean the action itself was unsuccessful if it produced useful discrimination.
Route performance shall be evaluated according to information gained, not merely whether the suspected failure was found.
Every material state change may trigger route recalculation.
ARIA shall calculate from the current state rather than return to the beginning of the original route.
Previously completed actions remain part of the current graph state.
Previously obtained valid evidence remains active unless invalidated.

required_capabilities: Explain why an action was selected.
Explain why a higher-probability hypothesis was not tested first.
Explain what information the action is expected to provide.
Explain which hypotheses the action discriminates between.
Explain operational costs or risks affecting route selection.
Explain when user history materially affected route selection.
Explain why an action was not repeated.

candidate_actions.action: Verify Main and Diversity physical RF routing

example_route.reason: Although RF routing is currently more probable, reviewing existing configuration provides substantial discrimination at negligible operational cost and may eliminate multiple competing hypotheses before physical tower work is requested.

ospf_analogy.description: ARIA's routing behavior is conceptually similar to dynamic network path selection but shall not literally implement OSPF metrics.

mapping.topology_change: new evidence or changed case state

ospf_analogy.important_difference: ARIA is navigating an uncertain information graph. The destination and graph topology may themselves be partially unknown until evidence is gathered.

semantic_rules.rule: The most probable diagnosis and the best next diagnostic action are separate calculations.
ARIA shall optimize expected diagnostic progress rather than blindly pursue the leading hypothesis.
Low-cost high-information actions should generally precede high-cost invasive actions when their diagnostic value is comparable.
Every diagnostic action shall have an identifiable purpose within the current reasoning state.
ARIA shall predict useful possible outcomes before selecting an action when practical.
Unexpected results shall become evidence and trigger rerouting.
ARIA shall reroute from the current state rather than restart a static troubleshooting sequence.
Previously completed diagnostic work shall remain represented in route state.
A diagnostic action that rules out a hypothesis may be highly successful even though it did not identify the final root cause.
ARIA shall penalize unjustified repetition of completed diagnostic actions.
Route costs and benefits may vary according to user, equipment, project phase, access, safety, service state, and available evidence.
User-specific routing shall optimize communication and execution efficiency without substituting historical user behavior for technical evidence.
Safety and authorization constraints may prohibit a route regardless of calculated diagnostic utility.
ARIA shall preserve sufficient routing history to reconstruct why each next hop was chosen.
Route-performance learning shall be context-sensitive and shall not convert one unsuccessful action into a universal prohibition.
When no available route provides sufficient expected value, ARIA shall seek additional context, broaden the hypothesis space, wait for required conditions, or escalate.
ARIA's routing graph shall be capable of expanding as new products, failure modes, diagnostic actions, and learned relationships are introduced.
The routing engine shall remain deterministic and auditable even when a language model assists in generating candidate actions.
No language-model recommendation shall bypass hard safety, authorization, or state-transition constraints.
The destination of diagnostic routing is not merely an answer; it is a sufficiently supported diagnosis, effective correction, and validated resolution.
